title: Critical Minerals
scope: Sourcing lithium, cobalt, nickel and rare earths for clean technology.

overview.summary: Battery and magnet minerals run through a few countries, mostly China; the central argument is over whether and how governments should change that.
overview.scope_covered: How lithium, nickel, cobalt, graphite, rare earths and copper are mined and refined, who controls each stage, what governments do about concentrated supply, how much new mining is needed against recycling and lower demand, and mining on Indigenous lands and the deep seabed.
overview.scope_excluded: How fast to decarbonize, firm power versus renewables and general trade policy, each on its own page; minerals mainly for chips and weapons, such as gallium and germanium, appear only as part of the supply-security story.
overview.why_now: At a Washington summit on September 23 to 25, 2026, Donald Trump and Xi Jinping extended by only two months, to January 10, 2027, the truce under which China suspended its October 2025 expansion of rare earth export controls.

stats.label: Share of world refining held by the top country, 2025
stats.note: In 2025 China refined 74 to 96 percent of the world’s lithium, cobalt, graphite, manganese and rare earths; Indonesia led nickel refining with 45 percent, ahead of China.
stats.detail: Mining is spread across many countries; refining, the chemical step that turns ore into battery-grade or magnet-grade material, is far more concentrated. The International Energy Agency puts the average share of the top refining country across key energy minerals at 70 percent in 2025, up from 68 percent in 2020, and reports that Indonesia (for nickel) and China (for the rest) supplied over three-quarters of all growth in refined output between 2023 and 2025. Rare earths were the one exception: new US projects and higher output in Malaysia cut China’s share from 91 percent in 2023 to 85 percent, which the agency credits to targeted policy and investment support. Indonesia’s nickel lead was built largely by Chinese-owned smelters. Export controls have opened price gaps: the IEA reports that gallium and the heavy rare earths dysprosium and terbium cost around five times more in Europe than on China’s domestic market.
stats.source_label: IEA, Global Critical Minerals Outlook 2026, Market overview

stats.label: Growth in critical mineral demand, 2025 to 2040
stats.note: Under policies governments have already adopted, the IEA projects demand for key critical minerals to almost double by 2040, with lithium demand more than tripling.
stats.detail: This is the IEA’s Stated Policies Scenario, which reflects adopted policies rather than climate targets, so faster decarbonization would raise these figures. For nickel, graphite and rare earths the projected growth is 1.5 to 1.9 times. Copper adds the most tonnage, about 7 million tonnes by 2040. Energy technologies drive most of the growth: the same 2026 outlook reports that the energy sector accounted for about 75 percent of demand growth across key energy minerals in 2025, and that global battery demand grew by over 35 percent that year to more than 1.5 terawatt-hours. Cobalt growth has slowed because cheaper lithium iron phosphate batteries, which use no cobalt or nickel, have taken a large share of the market. Projections are sensitive to battery chemistry and policy: the IEA’s 2021 critical minerals report found that cobalt demand in 2040 could range from 6 to 30 times its 2020 level depending on those assumptions.
stats.source_label: IEA, Global Critical Minerals Outlook 2026, Outlook

stats.label: Production outside China at risk from full rare earth export controls
stats.note: The IEA estimates that full implementation of China’s expanded rare earth export controls could put about $6.5 trillion a year of production outside China at risk.
stats.detail: The figure is the yearly value of downstream output in the automotive, high-tech, defense and energy sectors that depends on rare earth inputs, not an estimate of what would actually be lost; it shows how small volumes of minerals underpin very large industries. The IEA puts the comparable figure for a full disruption of battery-grade graphite at over $300 billion a year. China imposed licensing on seven medium and heavy rare earths in April 2025, forcing some automakers to cut production, and in October 2025 extended its proposed controls to foreign-made products containing Chinese-sourced rare earths or made with Chinese technology. As of September 2026 the October measures were suspended under the US-China truce and the April controls remained. China has also announced controls on battery cathode and anode materials and battery-making equipment, and by the IEA’s 2026 outlook the number of mineral tariff codes subject to its export controls had tripled since 2023.
stats.source_label: IEA, Global Critical Minerals Outlook 2026, Executive summary

stats.label: Mine supply expected in 2035 as a share of projected need
stats.note: On operating and announced projects, the IEA expects 2035 mine supply to meet about two-thirds of lithium needs and three-quarters of copper and cobalt needs; unannounced projects are not counted.
stats.detail: The percentages are calculated here from the IEA’s chart data: for lithium, 0.51 million tonnes of expected supply against 0.76 million tonnes of primary requirements; for copper, 20.7 against 27.3 million tonnes; for cobalt, 225 against 306 thousand tonnes. Primary requirements are total demand minus recycled supply, after refining losses. The IEA describes the gaps in the same terms: the projected 2035 copper deficit narrowed from about 30 percent in its 2025 report to 25 percent, while the cobalt gap widened from just over 15 percent to over 25 percent because the DRC’s export quotas are expected to cut supply. Its “high production” case, which adds early-stage projects, closes the nickel and graphite gaps. Whether the others close depends on how quickly higher prices call forth mines not yet planned, one of the questions below.
stats.source_label: IEA, Global Critical Minerals Outlook 2026, Outlook (percentages calculated from chart data)

stats.label: Transition mineral projects on or near Indigenous peoples’ lands
stats.note: More than half of the 5,097 energy transition mineral projects mapped in a 2023 study lie on or near Indigenous peoples’ lands.
stats.detail: Owen and colleagues geo-located every project with known reserves or resources. A third, 33 percent, are on or near peasant lands, and 69 percent are near one group or the other. By commodity, 85 percent of the lithium reserves and resources in the sample lie on or near Indigenous lands, and among early-stage projects, the ones still to be built, 68 percent are on or near Indigenous or peasant land.
stats.source_label: Owen et al., “Energy transition minerals and their intersection with land-connected peoples,” Nature Sustainability

stats.label: Price of battery-grade lithium carbonate, 2021 to 2025
stats.note: The average contract price of battery-grade lithium carbonate, adjusted for inflation, rose more than fivefold from 2021 to 2022 and then fell about 86 percent by 2025.
stats.detail: Prices spiked in 2022 as electric vehicle sales outran supply, drew a wave of new mines in Australia, China, Africa and South America, and collapsed as that supply arrived; the USGS reports world lithium output up 31 percent in 2025 alone. The bust closed or delayed many projects outside China, and the IEA’s 2026 outlook reports that lithium companies cut spending by around 40 percent in 2025. Prices then turned again: the same outlook reports that they more than doubled between January 2025 and April 2026, driven by demand for grid batteries and supply constraints. Those who favor price floors and stockpiles read this volatility as the reason markets alone underbuild supply outside China; those who oppose them read it as proof that high prices quickly bring forth new supply. The USGS price series comes from Benchmark Mineral Intelligence.
stats.source_label: US Geological Survey, Mineral Commodity Summaries 2026, Lithium

stats.label: Share of world mine output from the top producing country, 2025
stats.note: In 2025 the DRC mined about 73 percent of the world’s cobalt, China about 69 percent of its rare earths and Indonesia about two-thirds of its nickel; Australia led lithium with about a third.
stats.detail: The cobalt share is stated by the US Geological Survey; the others are calculated from its production tables (rare earths: China 270,000 of 390,000 tonnes of rare earth oxide; nickel: Indonesia 2.6 of 3.9 million tonnes; lithium: Australia 92,000 of 290,000 tonnes of lithium content, a world total that excludes withheld US output). In lithium, China (62,000 tonnes), Chile (56,000), Zimbabwe (28,000) and Argentina (23,000) follow. Mining and refining tell different stories: Australia refines only about 2 percent of the world’s lithium on the IEA’s 2025 chart, and the US mined about 13 percent of the world’s rare earths in 2025 yet still relied on imports for 67 percent of the rare earth compounds and metals it used, down from more than 95 percent in 2021 and 2022, according to the USGS rare earths chapter.
stats.source_label: US Geological Survey, Mineral Commodity Summaries 2026

stats.label: Public finance committed to critical minerals by advanced economies
stats.note: Governments of advanced economies committed about $65 billion of public finance to critical mineral projects in 2025, over four times the 2023 level, though disbursements lag far behind.
stats.detail: The money takes forms not seen in mining for decades. MP Materials announced in July 2025 that the US Defense Department would buy $400 million of its preferred stock and guarantee a price of $110 per kilogram for its neodymium-praseodymium oxide for ten years; the USGS puts the 2025 average market price at $69. E&E News reported in January 2026 that the Trump administration had also taken stakes in Lithium Americas, Trilogy Metals and USA Rare Earth. In February 2026 the State Department announced Project Vault, a civilian minerals stockpile backed by a loan of up to $10 billion from the Export-Import Bank and about $2 billion of private capital, and the European Commission’s RESourceEU plan of December 2025 commits up to €3 billion over 12 months. The IEA estimates that a strategic stockpile of the 11 highest-risk materials would cost countries outside the dominant supplier less than $900 million a year net. Private money moved the other way: the IEA reports that 24 major mining companies cut capital spending on critical minerals by 9 percent in 2025.
stats.source_label: IEA, Global Critical Minerals Outlook 2026, Executive summary

stats.label: DRC cobalt: mine output against the new export quota
stats.note: Under quotas set in October 2025, the DRC allows cobalt exports of up to 96,600 tonnes a year in 2026 and 2027, well under half of its 2025 mine output of about 230,000 tonnes.
stats.detail: In February 2025 the DRC temporarily banned cobalt exports, saying it wanted to address oversupply and low prices; in October it replaced the ban with quotas of 18,125 tonnes for the rest of 2025 and a yearly allowance for 2026 and 2027 that includes 9,600 tonnes for national strategic reserves. Mine output and exports are not the same thing, since ore can be stockpiled, so the comparison shows the scale of the restriction rather than an exact cut. The Cobalt Institute’s Cobalt Market Report 2025 records cobalt hydroxide prices rising by over 300 percent during 2025 and cobalt metal by 130 percent. The quotas sit alongside Indonesia’s ban on raw nickel ore exports, Zimbabwe’s restrictions on lithium ore and Mozambique’s on graphite. Artisanal mining, long associated with child labor in the DRC’s copper-cobalt belt, fell to less than 2 percent of DRC cobalt output in 2024 according to the industry-funded Cobalt Institute; its share rises when prices rise, and under the quotas legal artisanal output is capped through a state buyer allotted 470 tonnes a month.
stats.source_label: US Geological Survey, Mineral Commodity Summaries 2026, Cobalt

stats.label: Mineral inputs of an electric car compared with a conventional car
stats.note: The IEA found in 2021 that a typical electric car needs six times the mineral inputs of a conventional car, and an onshore wind plant nine times those of a gas-fired plant.
stats.detail: The new energy system front-loads its material needs into equipment, while the old one burns fuel continuously. The same report notes that this cuts both ways for security: a mineral shortage affects only new electric cars or solar plants, not those already running, while an oil shortage hits every gasoline car on the road; and minerals stay in equipment where they can later be recovered, while burned fuel cannot. It also found that over 50 percent of lithium and copper production was in areas of high water stress, and that average copper ore grades in Chile fell 30 percent over 15 years, meaning more rock, energy and water per tonne of metal. The comparison predates the rapid spread of lithium iron phosphate batteries, which contain no nickel or cobalt.
stats.source_label: IEA, The Role of Critical Minerals in Clean Energy Transitions, Executive summary

stats.label: Critical minerals as a share of the cost of finished products
stats.note: Critical minerals make up about 40 percent of what a permanent magnet costs and a quarter of a battery cell, but only about 3 percent of the price of an average electric vehicle.
stats.detail: The IEA also puts copper at 10 to 15 percent of the price of transformers and power cables, and rare earths at less than 1 percent of a vehicle’s value. These ratios underlie its case for a “mineral security premium”: on its estimates a tripling of rare earth prices would raise the cost of a car by about 0.1 percent, and a tripling of battery material prices would raise the price of electric vehicles and storage systems by about 5 percent. Intermediate producers are more exposed: battery cell makers and magnet makers outside China compete on thin margins, and the IEA reports that refining projects outside the dominant supplier cost 20 to over 150 percent more to build and about 50 percent more to operate. Opponents of subsidies and price floors read the same numbers differently: if users can absorb higher prices, they argue, users rather than taxpayers should pay them.
stats.source_label: IEA, Global Critical Minerals Outlook 2026, Executive summary

stats.label: Material mined per unit of electricity, solar against coal
stats.note: Counting fuel and the rock moved to reach materials, a 2024 study puts mining for solar power at about 45 tonnes per gigawatt-hour, onshore wind 59 and nuclear 10 to 13, against 1,179 for coal.
stats.detail: Seaver Wang and colleagues add two components, published by Our World in Data in kilograms per gigawatt-hour of lifetime output and rounded here: the metals and minerals used to build each plant, and rock, which for coal is the mined coal plus the waste rock moved to get it and for the others is the rock moved to extract their metals. Battery storage comes to about 40 tonnes and offshore wind about 35. Natural gas is not shown because its extraction is not comparable in this way. Hannah Ritchie of Our World in Data uses these figures to argue that a low-carbon energy system needs far less mining than a fossil one. The comparison measures tonnage, not harm: transition minerals are mined in smaller amounts but often in places with high water stress or Indigenous land claims, and per kilogram some are very rock-intensive, nickel at about 250 kilograms of rock per kilogram of metal by Ritchie’s count. Onshore wind’s higher total comes mainly from construction materials.
stats.source_label: Seaver Wang et al., “Updated Mining Footprints and Raw Material Needs for Clean Energy,” via Our World in Data

stats.label: Years from discovery to production for new mines
stats.note: S&P Global, in a 2024 study supported by the National Mining Association, puts US mine development at almost 29 years; an earlier S&P study of mines worldwide found 15.7.
stats.detail: The US figure assumes that projects in development for decades without producing will start by 2030, so it partly measures stalled projects; S&P noted that only three mines had come into production in the US since 2002, and states that the mining association provided no data or substantive input. The earlier S&P study covered 127 mines that opened worldwide from 2002 to 2023, which spent almost 12 of their years on exploration and studies, and the IEA’s 2021 report put the average at 16.5 years. Long lead times are the main argument for permitting reform and for acting before shortages appear. Those who defend environmental review argue that much of the delay comes from financing, price cycles and poorly designed projects rather than permits, and that litigation reflects real harms to water and land.
stats.source_label: S&P Global Market Intelligence, “Mine Development Times: The U.S. in Perspective”

stats.label: Countries calling for a pause on deep-sea mining
stats.note: As of August 2026, forty-six countries had called for a moratorium, precautionary pause or ban on mining the deep seabed.
stats.detail: The seabed of the Clarion-Clipperton Zone in the Pacific holds potato-sized polymetallic nodules rich in nickel, cobalt, manganese and copper; the USGS Mineral Commodity Summaries 2026 estimate that seafloor nodules worldwide hold about 5 billion tonnes of cobalt and, citing a 2022 USGS study, that seabed deposits hold about 4.5 billion tonnes of nickel, far more than land reserves. Mining in international waters is governed by the International Seabed Authority, which in 2026 had 172 members (171 states and the European Union) and had issued exploration contracts covering 31 areas; Mongabay reported that its July 2026 session again ended without adopting the regulations needed to allow commercial mining. The United States, which never ratified the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea, issued an executive order in April 2025 to develop seabed minerals under its own 1980 law, and as of September 2026 NOAA was reviewing The Metals Company’s application for the first commercial recovery permit.
stats.source_label: Deep Sea Conservation Coalition, “Momentum for a moratorium”

stats.label: Cut in new mine needs from recycling by 2050
stats.note: If climate pledges are met, the IEA sees recycling cutting 2050 mine needs 40 percent for copper and cobalt, 25 percent for lithium and nickel; Earthworks finds larger copper and nickel cuts by 2040.
stats.detail: Recycling cannot supply a fast-growing market from scrap that does not exist yet: electric vehicle batteries last a decade or more, so the IEA expects manufacturing scrap to be two-thirds of recycling feedstock in 2030 and end-of-life batteries to take over only after 2035. It projects recycled battery metals reaching 20 to 30 percent of lithium, nickel and cobalt demand by 2050, depending on collection rates, and says recycled nickel, cobalt and lithium produce about 80 percent less greenhouse gas than mined material. China held about 80 percent of global battery pretreatment and material recovery capacity in 2023, and end-of-life collection of rare earth magnets is below 15 percent. A 2021 study for the advocacy group Earthworks by the University of Technology Sydney estimated cuts by 2040 of 55 percent for copper, 35 percent for cobalt and nickel and 25 percent for lithium, and argued that reducing private car ownership is essential to limiting new mining.
stats.source_label: IEA, Recycling of Critical Minerals, Executive summary

stats.label: Lithium-ion battery pack prices, 2025
stats.note: Battery pack prices fell 8 percent in 2025 to an average $108 per kilowatt-hour even as battery metal prices rose; packs that use no nickel or cobalt averaged $81.
stats.detail: Lithium iron phosphate (LFP) packs need no nickel or cobalt, and the shift toward them is one of the main reasons projected demand for those two metals has fallen; the IEA reports that LFP made up around 40 percent of electric vehicle batteries deployed in 2023. BloombergNEF reports that prices in North America and Europe were 44 and 56 percent higher than in China, and that metal price increases in 2025, including from the DRC’s cobalt quotas, did not raise pack prices because cell manufacturing has excess capacity. Chemistry change cuts both ways for supply security: it reduces dependence on the DRC’s cobalt and Indonesia’s nickel, but LFP cathode production is itself concentrated in China, and lithium and graphite are still needed.

stats.label: Indonesia’s processed nickel exports since its raw ore ban
stats.note: After Indonesia banned raw nickel ore exports, its exports of processed nickel rose from about $1 billion a year at their pre-ban peak to about $15 billion in 2023 and $13.2 billion in 2024.
stats.detail: Indonesia first banned raw ore exports in January 2014, relaxed the ban in 2017 for lower-grade ore and reimposed it fully in 2020, forcing miners to process ore at home. Chinese companies built most of the smelters, and the CETEx authors report that more than 90 percent of the resulting ferronickel and alloy exports went to China in 2024 and that Indonesia’s share of world nickel production has exceeded 50 percent since 2023. They also report that nickel companies cleared more than 75,000 hectares of forest between 2007 and 2022, that the processing hubs in Central Sulawesi and North Maluku run largely on new captive coal power plants, and that most smelter output goes to stainless steel rather than batteries. In a case brought by the European Union, a World Trade Organization panel ruled in November 2022 that the ban violated WTO rules; Indonesia appealed to the WTO’s Appellate Body, which has lacked a quorum since 2019, so as of March 2026 the ruling had not taken effect.
stats.source_label: Utamawati & Yusuf, CETEx, London School of Economics, from Statistics Indonesia data

questions.text: Should governments pay to build mineral supply outside China, or leave sourcing to markets and trade?
questions.why: Everyone agrees supply is concentrated. The dispute is whether that is a market failure only the state can fix or a risk that prices, private inventories and trade will manage, and so whether public money spent on it is insurance or waste.
questions.detail:
Those who would pay argue that China built its position over decades with state finance and can flood a market to bankrupt rivals, then restrict exports when it wants leverage, so no private investor will rationally build a refinery outside China without guaranteed prices, offtake contracts or stockpiles behind it. Because minerals are a small share of what finished products cost, they say, the premium is cheap insurance against disruptions that could idle whole industries.

Those who would leave it to markets answer that past supply scares ended with new sources, new chemistries and lower prices within a few years. Government equity stakes and guaranteed prices, they say, pick winners in technical industries officials do not understand, invite cronyism and leave taxpayers holding losses when prices fall. They would rather remove obstacles governments created themselves, above all permitting delays, trade freely with allies and let manufacturers that want security pay for inventory and diversified supply. Where each person lands depends on how likely and how damaging a cutoff is, partly a judgment about China’s intentions and partly one about the proper role of the state.

questions.text: Will mine supply keep pace with clean-technology demand through the 2030s?
questions.why: Projections show gaps, but forecasts of mineral markets have repeatedly been wrong in both directions. The answer turns on how fast prices call forth new mines, how long those take to open, and how fast chemistry and recycling shift demand.
questions.detail:
Those who expect shortfalls note that mines take well over a decade from discovery to production, so supply for the mid-2030s must be found and financed in the 2020s, yet the IEA reports that exploration for lithium and nickel fell by about 40 percent in 2025. Ore grades are falling, copper deposits are deeper and poorer, many new deposits lie in water-stressed places or on Indigenous lands where projects stall, and export quotas or controls can remove supply overnight. A shortage would raise the cost of the energy transition and slow it.

Those who expect supply to adapt point to lithium, where the 2022 price spike produced a glut within two years. Geological resources are ample: the USGS puts identified lithium resources at about 150 million tonnes. Projected gaps count only projects already announced, and higher prices call forth more. Chemistry shifts, such as lithium iron phosphate batteries that use no cobalt or nickel and sodium-ion batteries that use no lithium, cut demand for whichever mineral becomes scarce.

questions.text: Should communities be able to block a mine on their land?
questions.why: The UN Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples sets a standard of free, prior and informed consent, but many governments read it as a duty to consult, not a right to refuse. How much local consent should weigh against national needs is a value choice.
questions.detail:
Those who would give communities a veto argue that mining reshapes land, water and livelihoods for generations, that the people who bear those costs have historically been overridden, and that a right to consent that cannot include saying no is not a right. Projects pushed through without consent, they say, end in conflict, litigation and delay anyway, while those that win genuine consent through shared ownership and benefits last longer, and a transition built on dispossession erodes public support for itself.

Those who hold that consultation is enough argue that the energy transition and national security serve millions of people, including future generations exposed to climate change, and that no single community should be able to block resources a whole country needs. Elected governments weigh these interests through permitting and environmental review, with mitigation and benefit-sharing for those affected. A universal veto, they warn, would make many deposits unminable and push production to countries where no one is consulted at all.

questions.text: Will China keep its leverage over mineral supply, or does using it erode its own position?
questions.why: China has restricted exports of gallium, germanium, graphite, antimony and rare earths since 2023 and suspended only some limits in a truce. Whether its leverage lasts depends on how fast others build processing and on what restriction costs China.
questions.detail:
Those who see lasting leverage argue that China’s hold is not in ore but in processing know-how, equipment and scale that took decades to build, which Beijing now protects with bans on exporting the technology itself. The IEA reports that planned magnet production outside the dominant supplier is only about a third of the rare earths expected to be mined by 2035. China can calibrate its controls, licensing some buyers and not others, which keeps the threat alive even while restrictions are suspended; Al Jazeera reported that in June 2026 it added two US rare earth companies to its export control list.

Those who see a self-defeating weapon argue that each use speeds the alternatives that erode it: the 2025 controls set off tens of billions of dollars of Western public finance, Chinese producers lose revenue and customers when controls bite, and buyers design restricted materials out of their products. Over a decade, on this view, the threat shrinks the market share that makes it credible.

questions.text: Do bans on raw mineral exports help producer countries develop?
questions.why: Indonesia’s nickel ore ban is the leading test and is read both ways, as an industrial success or as a windfall for foreign smelter owners. The DRC, Zimbabwe and others are trying versions of it, so the answer bears on much of world supply.
questions.detail:
Those who think bans work argue that exporting raw ore keeps poor countries at the bottom of the value chain, where they earn the least and absorb the most damage, and that every rich country industrialized behind policies to capture more value at home. Indonesia’s ban, in this reading, made it the world’s leading nickel processor within a few years and drew tens of billions of dollars of investment that would otherwise have gone to China.

Those who think bans backfire argue that they work only for countries with a dominant share of a mineral and the capital to attract processors, and that even then the gains go mostly to the foreign firms that build the plants. Bans invite retaliation and legal challenge, deter mining investment and push buyers toward substitutes; high nickel prices helped make batteries without nickel or cobalt attractive. Better royalties, transparent contracts and investment in skills, they argue, deliver more value with less risk.

questions.text: Should the mineral demands of clean technology slow its deployment?
questions.why: Clean technologies need more minerals to build than the fossil systems they replace, and much supply runs through China. Whether that argues for slower targets or faster supply chains turns on how dependence and mining harms weigh against climate risk.
questions.detail:
Those who would slow the build-out argue that mandating a switch to electric vehicles and renewables on a fixed timetable hands demand to supply chains China dominates, raising costs and creating strategic vulnerability, and makes wealthy countries accept mining damage abroad they would not accept at home. They would let consumers and utilities choose, rely on domestic oil, gas and nuclear power in the meantime, and adopt more moderate targets so that mineral supply can grow at a sustainable pace.

Those who would keep building fast argue that per unit of electricity, wind and solar need far less mining than coal once the fuel is counted, and that minerals stay in equipment to be recycled while fossil fuels are dug up and burned continuously. Climate damage compounds with every year of delay, and the countries that build clean industries now will lead them. Dependence on China, they say, is a reason to build supply chains faster, not to stay dependent on oil and gas markets that have chokepoints of their own.

questions.text: How far can recycling, new battery chemistries and lower demand cut the need for new mines?
questions.why: Recycling and substitution are central to the case that the transition can proceed with far less mining, but batteries last a decade or more, so scrap arrives after demand has grown. Estimates turn on collection rates, car ownership and chemistry.
questions.detail:
Those who expect deep cuts argue that, unlike burned fuel, metals in a battery or magnet can be recovered, and that the IEA already finds recycling rates for nickel and cobalt above 40 percent of available feedstock. Smaller vehicles, more public transit and longer product lives could cut demand further, and chemistry has moved fast before: batteries without cobalt or nickel went from a niche to a large share of the electric car market within a few years. Planning for maximum mining, on this view, locks in harms that smarter demand policy would avoid.

Those who expect mining to remain dominant answer that demand is growing far faster than scrap can accumulate, so recycling will cover only a minority of supply for decades, and the IEA says new mines remain essential. Lower car ownership is a social choice most countries have not made, and substitution moves dependence rather than ending it, since lithium iron phosphate cathodes and battery recycling capacity are both concentrated in China.

questions.text: Should commercial mining of the deep seabed begin?
questions.why: Seabed nodules could supply nickel and cobalt without clearing forests or displacing anyone, but the ecosystems they lie in are among the least studied on Earth. Science can narrow that uncertainty; how much risk to accept before it does is a value choice.
questions.detail:
Those who would begin argue that land mining for nickel and cobalt clears rainforest, relies on coal power and in the DRC has involved child labor, while nodules sit loose on the seafloor with no overburden to remove and no people to displace. The nodules hold enough metal to break the concentration of supply in a few countries, decades of exploration and test collection have produced environmental data, and regulation can require monitoring and set aside protected zones. Waiting for perfect knowledge, they say, means continuing the known harms of land mining.

Those who would pause first argue that deep-sea ecosystems recover over centuries if at all, that most species in the Clarion-Clipperton Zone have not yet been described, and that sediment plumes from collection could spread far beyond mined areas. The minerals are not urgently needed, they say, because battery chemistry is moving away from cobalt and nickel and recycling is growing, and a unilateral US permit would undermine the international system that treats the seabed as the common heritage of humankind.

positions.name: Build supply chains outside China with state backing
positions.steelman: China has shown it will cut off the minerals modern industry runs on, and markets will not fix that alone; democracies must finance, buy and stockpile new supply together.
positions.detail:
Critical minerals are now what oil was in the 1970s: the input everything else depends on, controlled by a supplier willing to cut it off for political ends. China did not win this market on cost alone. It spent decades building refining and magnet capacity with state finance, priced rivals out, and showed with its 2025 rare earth controls that it will use the result as leverage. No private investor will build a refinery that China can bankrupt by flooding the market. So democracies must do what China did, quickly and together: guarantee prices and offtake for new projects, take equity where needed, hold strategic stockpiles, speed permits and pool demand among allies so that diversified supply has buyers. Targeted support already works: China’s share of rare earth refining has begun to fall where we have invested.

Free-market critics say state stakes and price floors breed cronyism and copy the model we oppose. The alternative has been tried: decades of leaving minerals to the market produced today’s dependence, because the market China operates in is not free. Price floors and offtake contracts are standard tools where a state actor distorts prices, the sums are small next to defense and industrial budgets, and transparency and competitive tenders can guard against favoritism. Our US wing frames this as national and economic security, extends it to minerals for AI, chips and weapons, and backs tariffs and deep-sea mining under US law. Our European wing frames it as part of the green and digital transitions, sets 2030 targets for domestic mining, processing and recycling, and puts more weight on environmental standards.
positions.proponents: US Department of State; European Commission; Government of Japan; Government of Australia; Government of Canada; G7 Critical Minerals Production Alliance; MP Materials; Gracelin Baskaran

positions.name: Process minerals in the countries that mine them
positions.steelman: Countries that hold the minerals should keep the value: refine and manufacture at home, and make every buyer, Chinese or Western, invest here on those terms.
positions.detail:
For a century, resource-rich countries in Africa, Asia and Latin America exported ore and imported the finished goods made from it, keeping the low-value, high-damage end of the chain while refining, manufacturing and jobs went elsewhere. The energy transition is our chance to break that pattern, and the leverage to do it is in the ground. Countries that hold the minerals should require processing at home through export bans, quotas, local-content rules or state partnerships, and negotiate with every buyer on that basis. The new Western interest in “secure supply chains” is welcome only if it means investment in our industry, not a new scramble for raw materials on old terms. Like oil producers before us, we have the right to manage the supply and price of resources we own. As Indonesia’s deputy investment minister, Todotua Pasaribu, told the Antara news agency in February 2026, “those eyeing our mineral sector must invest in processing, as our law forbids exports of raw products.”

We are told that bans mainly enrich foreign smelter owners, damage the environment, deter investment and break trade rules. Every industrial power, including those now objecting, protected its infant industries, and WTO rules written by importing countries are not a neutral standard. The remedy for polluting, foreign-dominated smelters is better domestic regulation, partnerships and ownership requirements, not a return to exporting ore. Our instruments differ: Indonesia and Zimbabwe ban raw exports, the DRC uses quotas and is building a battery-precursor industry with Zambia, Chile and Bolivia rely on state control of lithium, and the African Union’s Green Minerals Strategy stresses regional value chains, fair contracts and revenue transparency over bans.
positions.proponents: African Union; Government of Indonesia; Government of the Democratic Republic of the Congo; Government of Zimbabwe; Government of Chile; UN Secretary-General’s Panel on Critical Energy Transition Minerals

positions.name: Cut mineral demand and mine only with consent
positions.steelman: A clean transition built on dispossession is neither just nor durable: need less new mining, recycle what we already have, and let affected communities say no.
positions.detail:
The clean energy transition is necessary, but one that repeats the extractive injustices of the fossil fuel era will not last. Transition minerals lie disproportionately on Indigenous and peasant lands, often where water is scarce, conflict is common or governance is weak, and the rush for supply is already overriding communities: Amnesty International reported in May 2026 that three lithium projects in Nevada went ahead without the consent of affected tribes. The answer is to need less new mining and to mine better: design for reuse and recycling, invest in public transit and smaller vehicles rather than replacing every gasoline car with a heavy electric one, and require binding human rights and environmental due diligence. Where mining happens, affected communities, above all Indigenous peoples, must be able to give or withhold consent, and some places, including the deep seabed and sacred and ecologically critical lands, should be off limits.

We are told that demand cannot fall fast enough and that a community veto would push mining to places with no protections at all. But projects imposed over local opposition are delayed for years by litigation and protest, so consent is faster in the end, and binding due diligence laws in consuming countries, such as the European Union’s, reach supply chains wherever mining takes place. We do not oppose all new mining; we oppose mining without consent and mining that destroys irreplaceable places. Human rights groups such as Amnesty focus on consent, labor rights and due diligence and accept that new mining is needed; environmental and degrowth-minded groups put more weight on cutting consumption, especially private car ownership; marine conservation groups lead the campaign for a deep-sea moratorium.
positions.proponents: Earthworks; Amnesty International; Deep Sea Conservation Coalition; Greenpeace; WWF; SIRGE Coalition

positions.name: Keep mineral trade open and let markets supply
positions.steelman: Concentration is real, but state stakes and price floors repeat industrial policy’s old mistakes; fix permitting, trade freely with allies, and let buyers pay for their own security.
positions.detail:
The remedy now in fashion, governments taking equity stakes, guaranteeing prices and running stockpiles, repeats the mistakes of past industrial policy and imitates the Chinese state capitalism it claims to resist. Officials do not know which rare earth startup or lithium project will succeed, and when the White House picks winners, capital flows to the politically connected rather than the most capable. Price floors set above the market create surpluses and taxpayer losses. Markets have answered supply scares before: after China restricted rare earth exports in 2010, buyers found other sources and China dropped the restrictions in 2015 after losing a World Trade Organization case, and lithium’s 2022 price spike produced a glut. What keeps Western supply small is government itself: decades-long permitting, litigation and rules that make processing uneconomic. Fix those, trade freely with allies, and let companies that need security pay for inventory and diversified contracts.

We are told China is not a market actor, so leaving supply to the market means leaving it to Beijing. That justifies targeted, transparent tools, such as buying magnets for defense through procurement contracts, modest stockpiles for genuine military needs and trade agreements with allies, not government ownership of private companies or open-ended price guarantees. China’s leverage erodes each time it is used, and the costs of industrial policy are not only fiscal: corruption, misallocated capital and higher prices for every downstream manufacturer weaken the economy that security depends on. Some of us, like Tad DeHaven of the Cato Institute, accept defense procurement and stockpiles but not equity stakes; others oppose the Project Vault stockpile too.
positions.proponents: Cato Institute; Tad DeHaven; Scott Lincicome; Veronique de Rugy; Mercatus Center; Wall Street Journal editorial board

positions.name: Scale back the clean-energy mandates driving mineral demand
positions.steelman: The mineral crunch is self-inflicted: stop forcing a fast switch to electric cars and renewables that hands China leverage, and let consumer choice and secure supply set the pace.
positions.detail:
Governments mandated a rapid switch to electric vehicles, wind and solar, each of which needs several times more minerals than what it replaces, and then discovered that China controls the supply chains those mandates depend on. Forcing the pace hands demand, jobs and leverage to Beijing, raises the cost of energy and vehicles, and accepts mining damage abroad that rich countries would not tolerate at home, while mines take decades to open and announced projects fall short of projected needs even under policies already adopted. The sensible course is to stop mandating and subsidizing particular technologies, let consumers and utilities choose, keep using domestic oil, gas and nuclear power, and let mineral-intensive technologies grow at the pace markets and secure supply can sustain. Domestic mining should be permitted quickly, but not to feed a timetable set by climate targets.

We are told that delay costs more in climate damage than it saves, and that fossil fuels need far more mining per unit of energy. Tonnage comparisons miss the point: coal and gas come from many suppliers, often domestic or allied, while battery and magnet minerals run through a single strategic rival. Emissions from the United States and Europe are a shrinking share of the world total, so slowing their mandates changes the climate little while making them less dependent on China, and nuclear power, which needs the least mining of any source, offers a cleaner path. The Heritage Foundation and its allies want electric vehicle and renewable mandates and subsidies repealed outright; Mark P. Mills of the National Center for Energy Analytics accepts that wind, solar and batteries will grow but argues for slower targets. Many of us back tariffs and domestic mining for defense and industrial minerals.
positions.proponents: Heritage Foundation; Mark P. Mills; National Center for Energy Analytics; Institute for Energy Research; Diana Furchtgott-Roth

crux.lead: Is concentrated mineral supply a passing market condition or a lasting vulnerability, and who pays to fix it?
crux.lead_highlight: a passing market condition or a lasting vulnerability
crux.subtitle: Almost everyone agrees the minerals in batteries, magnets and power grids come from too few places. The split is over whether prices, trade and new technology will spread supply on their own, and if not, whether taxpayers, mining communities or the climate should bear the cost of changing it.
crux.empirical: Much of this can be measured: how fast supply outside the dominant producers responds to price without subsidy, whether state-backed projects reach production at competitive cost, whether repeated export controls build alternatives faster than they do damage, how far recycling and new battery chemistries cut the need for new mines in the 2030s, and how much harm seabed mining does. Each finding would move people between camps.
crux.values: The rest does not share a unit: the speed of decarbonization against the consent of people living on the deposits, national security against open trade, producer countries’ claim to industry against importers’ wish for cheap supply, the known harms of mining on land against the unknown harms at sea. Evidence can show what each policy costs and whom it affects, not whose costs should count most.

primary_image_prompt:
A minimalist flat vector-style icon illustration, in a clean editorial line-art style: a large faceted chunk of raw ore with a few crystal points as the dominant focal mass in the foreground; behind it a terraced open-pit mine of medium size cut into a rounded hill, its stepped benches overlapping the ore's back edge; a small haul truck on one of the benches; a conveyor belt on slim legs running diagonally across the whole frame from the pit down to a small upright cylindrical battery cell at the lower right as the connective element; the ground is a gentle rolling curve.

Composition: one dominant focal mass with smaller supporting elements at clearly different scales (big, medium, small); at least one element overlaps another so the scene has depth; the ground is a gentle curve, never a flat line; one connective element runs across the frame to tie the pieces together. A single coherent scene, not a row of separate objects. Centered with generous, even padding.

Style: monoline line art with ONE uniform stroke weight on every element, including the thinnest wisps and lines. Rounded line caps and corners. Confident, slightly bold strokes so it stays legible when small. No fussy internal detail.

Color: a single hue, two tones only. Draw all lines in solid #3f9a6a, and give every major mass a clearly visible soft fill of the same hue at about 15-18% opacity, so the duotone is obviously present rather than white interiors. No other colors, no gradients, no shadows, no 3D, no texture.

Important: NO border, NO frame, NO box or outline around the scene, just the illustration on a plain white background. No text, letters, or numbers. No human figures or faces. Calm, neutral, editorial mood: show the subject plainly, neither celebrating nor warning. Also avoid: flags, national symbols, maps, dragons, children or workers, chains, shackles, skulls, smoke, dust clouds, money or coin symbols, cracked earth, polluted water, gold bars, padlocks, arrows, warning signs.
